criterion_notes.c1: Examines household access and connection to the formal piped water network in peripheral, unauthorized settlements ('revenue layouts') of Greater Bangalore under the Greater Bangalore Water and Sanitation Project (GBWASP).
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it analyzes municipal/utility water sector governance and cost-recovery reforms. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly examines concrete rule-type mechanisms governing piped water connection access: (1) a mandatory 'beneficiary capital contribution' tariff/cost-recovery rule ($60 to $375 tiered by property dimensions) coupled with monthly late-payment enforcement penalties ($1 to $8/month after the deadline), and (2) documentation and land-tenure eligibility requirements for informal 'revenue layout' properties, including the utility's administrative accommodation/waiver removing formal proof of land tenure as an eligibility prerequisite for a water connection and meter once payment receipts for pipes were shown.
criterion_notes.c3: Mixed-methods socio-legal/ethnographic and quantitative empirical study conducted in 2007-2009, combining 50 in-depth interviews with utility engineers and state technocrats, 44 semi-structured interviews with peripheral residents and resident welfare associations (RWAs), archival document/petition analysis, and a quantitative survey of 1,864 household payment receipts from Bommanahalli municipal records compared against household income survey data (n = 8,000).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports multiple access-relevant outcomes at the household and settlement levels: upfront connection affordability/cost burden (average capital contribution of $260 per household including penalties, equal to 100% of average monthly household income and ranging from 70% to 160%, with some households unable to afford payment), removal of formal tenure documentation as an eligibility barrier for connection/metering, and actual piped water delivery/availability delays (80% of Bangalore's outskirts still lacking piped water access via the project years after paying).
criterion_notes.c5: Population (households/property owners in informal 'revenue layouts' at Bangalore's periphery, specifically Bommanahalli zone; n = 1,864 household payment receipts, 44 resident interviews, 50 official interviews), exposure (beneficiary capital contribution cost-recovery rule, late-payment penalties, and land-tenure eligibility/waiver rules), outcome (upfront affordability burden relative to income, connection eligibility without formal title, and piped water delivery/access), and mixed-methods case study design are all clearly identified.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: In 2003, the city of Bangalore in the southern Indian state of Karnataka launched the Greater Bangalore water project to connect over a million peripheral residents to the piped water network.

Under the new policy, peripheral residents were required to pay between $60 and $375 towards the capital costs of network expansion (mainly for feeder lines and distribution pipes) based on the dimensions of their properties
In other words, as a result of RWAs’ political maneuverings, formal tenure was successfully removed as an eligibility requirement for actual service delivery.
This article stems from a larger multi-sited ethnography on the politics of water reforms in peripheral Bangalore, research for which was conducted between 2007 and 2009.

Surveying 1,864 receipts from one ward in Bommanahalli, I found that on average, residents contributed a one-time amount of over $260 per household (see Table 1). On average, this translated into roughly one full month’s household income and at times as high as one and a half times one month’s income.
That said, not all peripheral households contributed; some could not afford to pay and others preferred to wait until the water arrived.

raw_response.exposure: Mandatory upfront 'beneficiary capital contribution' cost-recovery rule ($60-$375 tiered by property area) with monthly late-payment enforcement penalties ($1-$8/month), and land-tenure documentation/eligibility rules (including the BWSSB's waiver of formal proof of tenure in favor of payment receipts as proof of residence for water connection and meter eligibility).
raw_response.outcome: Household upfront connection cost/affordability burden (average payment of $260 or 100% of monthly household income across 1,864 receipts; exclusion/non-payment among households unable to afford the charge), eligibility for formal water connection and meter without formal land title, and piped water service availability/delivery across peripheral settlements.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Households and informal 'revenue layout' property owners ('peripheralized middle class') and state/utility actors in peripheral Greater Bangalore (primarily Bommanahalli zone), India; n = 1,864 household payment receipts surveyed in one Bommanahalli ward (compared with n = 8,000 household income survey), 44 semi-structured resident/RWA interviews, and 50 interviews with utility engineers, bureaucrats, and technocrats.
raw_response.rationale: This mixed-methods empirical study examines household access to piped water in informal peripheral settlements ('revenue layouts') of Bangalore, India under the Greater Bangalore Water and Sanitation Project. It directly investigates rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms governing service access under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 reading of Criterion 2 — specifically upfront capital cost-recovery charges tiered by plot size, monthly late-payment penalties, and land-tenure documentation requirements (including an administrative waiver allowing capital contribution receipts to substitute for formal tenure proof in securing water connections and meters) — and reports quantitative and qualitative evidence on household affordability burdens, eligibility, and piped water availability. All inclusion criteria (c1-c6) are met.
raw_response.study_design: Mixed-methods empirical case study (multi-sited ethnography, semi-structured interviews, and archival household payment receipt survey)
